## Libraries and data load

Put whatever libraries you use here.

```{r}
#| label: setup 
#| include: false
#| library(tidyverse)
#| library(tidymodels)
#| library(kknn)
```

Load your data here

```{r}
# Data Compiled in separate QMD (Submitted in an earlier assignment)
FullData_2025 <- read.csv("Data/FullData_2025.csv")
```

```{r}
# Clean Data [Helpful for graphs and Models]
FullData_2025 <- FullData_2025|>
  drop_na()

# Make response variable a Factor [Helpful for LOGISTIC REG]
FullData_2025<-FullData_2025|>
  mutate(Democracy=as.factor(Democracy))
```

**NOTE REGARDING DATA:** Please note that the data for each variable was collected from the last year provided in their respective datasets. For our purposes, we will be treated all variables as being collected from the year 2025 regardless of their most recent data. Below are the *actual* years each column was collected from:

*Democracy:* 2020

*CO2 Emissions:* 2022

*GDP per Capita:* 2025

*Human Development Index:* 2023

*People in Poverty:* 2025

*Gapminder Regions:* 2025

## Exploratory data analysis

For this section graph and find statistics for each of your predictor variables vs the response. You do not need to look at the predictor variables individually


## Variable 1: CO2 Emissions

### Graph and description

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| fig-align: center  

#PLOT
FullData_2025 |>
  ggplot(aes(x = CO2, y = Democracy)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::comma) +# using log because you cant see the data regularly
  labs(x = "CO2 emissions (Million Tonnes, log scale)",
       y = "Democracy",
       title = "Democracy in 2025 vs. CO2 Emissions")
```

This boxplot compares CO2 emissions, in million tonnes, for democracies and non-democracies. The x axis is on a log scale, so each step to the right is 10 times bigger. The democracy box is farther to the right. The median is about 48 for democracies and about 14 for non-democracies. The middle half of democracies goes from about 14 to 200. For non-democracies, it goes from about 4 to 42. The boxes overlap a lot, so many countries in both groups have similar emissions. Still, the typical democracy emits more, and democracies are more spread out. Their whiskers go from about 0.6 up to about 5,500, and the USA is at the far end. Non-democracies go from about 0.2 up to about 700. They have one outlier at about 1,440, which is Russia. The log scale makes the biggest values look smaller than they are, so the table shows the real numbers. Overall, democracies tend to emit more CO2, but the two groups overlap a lot.The groups overlap a lot, so CO2 would not predict democracy well by itself.

### Stats and description

```{r}

Democracy_CO2_summary <- FullData_2025 |>
  group_by(Democracy) |>
  summarize(avg_co2 = mean(CO2 ),
            sd_co2 = sd(CO2),
            min_co2 = min(CO2),
            max_co2 = max(CO2),
            mdn_co2 = median(CO2),
            iqr_co2 = IQR(CO2),
            count = n())

Democracy_CO2_summary

FullData_2025 |># to find more information on the data
  arrange(desc(CO2)) |>
  select(name, Democracy, CO2) |>
  head(8)
```

This table shows CO2 emissions, in million tonnes, for 73 democracies and 85 non-democracies. Democracies emit more. Their mean is about 256.2, and the mean for non-democracies is about 73.4. The medians show the same thing, at about 48.4 for democracies and about 14.1 for non-democracies. In both groups, the mean is about five times bigger than the median. This means a few very big emitters pull the means up, so the median shows a typical country better. Democracies are also more spread out. Their standard deviation is about 729.3 and their IQR is about 183.6. For non-democracies, these are about 193.2 and 37.0. The smallest values are tiny in both groups, about 0.6 for democracies and about 0.2 for non-democracies. The biggest values are very different. The top democracy is the USA at about 5,563.7. The top non-democracy is Russia at about 1,442.5. China is missing from the data, so the non-democracy numbers are probably too low. Overall, democracies tend to emit more CO2 and vary more, but this shows a link, not a cause.

## Variable 2: GDP per Capita

### Graph and description

```{r}
FullData_2025|>
  ggplot(aes(x = GDP, y = Democracy)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::comma)+ # removes the statistical notation in the x axis
  labs(x = "GDP per Capita in (US dollars)",
       y = "Democracy",
       title = "Democracy in 2025 vs. GDP per Capita, 2025)")
```

This boxplot compares GDP per capita, in US dollars, for democracies and non-democracies. The democracy box is far to the right of the non-democracy box. The median is about 42,000 for democracies and about 7,000 for non-democracies. The middle half of democracies goes from about 19,000 to 56,000. For non-democracies, it goes from about 3,000 to 15,000. The two boxes barely overlap, so most democracies are richer per person than most non-democracies. Democracies are also more spread out, because their box is much wider. Both groups have outliers on the high end. Democracies have three, from about 120,000 to 138,000. Non-democracies have six, from about 37,000 to 65,000. Some of these non-democracies are richer than the typical democracy. The non-democracy group is more skewed to the right, with most countries bunched on the left and a few rich ones far out. Overall, democracies tend to have a much higher GDP per capita. The boxes barely overlap, so GDP separates the groups well, but it is skewed.

### Stats and description

```{r}
Democracy_GDP_summary <- FullData_2025 |>
  group_by(Democracy) |>
  summarize(avg_gdp = mean(GDP),
            sd_gdp = sd(GDP),
            min_gdp = min(GDP),
            max_gdp = max(GDP),
            mdn_gdp = median(GDP),
            iqr_gdp = IQR(GDP),
            count = n())

Democracy_GDP_summary
```

This table shows GDP per capita, in US dollars, for 73 democracies and 85 non-democracies. Democracies are much richer per person. Their mean is about 42,602, and the mean for non-democracies is about 11,740. That is about 3.6 times higher. The medians show an even bigger gap, at about 41,978 for democracies and about 7,143 for non-democracies. So the typical democracy has a GDP per capita almost six times higher. For democracies, the mean and median are almost the same, so the values are fairly balanced. For non-democracies, the mean is well above the median, and the standard deviation (about 12,864) is bigger than the mean. This means a few rich non-democracies pull the average up, while most are much poorer. Democracies are also more spread out. Their standard deviation is about 28,554 and their IQR is about 36,811. For non-democracies, these are about 12,864 and 11,758. The ranges overlap. The poorest democracy is at about 2,716, and the richest non-democracy is at about 64,966. That means some non-democracies are richer than the typical democracy. The richest democracy is at about 137,906, which is more than twice the richest non-democracy. Overall, democracies tend to have a much higher GDP per capita, but this shows a link, not a cause.

## Variable 3: Human Development Index

### Graph and description

```{r}
FullData_2025|>
  ggplot(aes(x = HDI, y = Democracy)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(x = "Human Development Index",
       y = "Democracy",
       title = "Democracy in 2025 vs. Human Development Index")
```

This boxplot compares the Human Development Index (HDI) for democracies (Yes) and non-democracies (No). HDI is a score from 0 to 1, and a higher score means higher development. The democracy box sits far to the right of the non-democracy box. The median line for democracies is at about 0.88, and for non-democracies it is at about 0.63. The two boxes barely overlap. The democracy box runs from about 0.78 to 0.93, and the non-democracy box runs from about 0.52 to 0.75. The democracy box is narrower, so democracies are more alike in their scores. The non-democracy box is wider, so those countries vary more. The democracy median sits close to the right side of its box, and the lower whisker is long, reaching down to about 0.55. This shows that most democracies score high, with a few lower scorers. The non-democracy median is near the middle of its box, so the scores are spread more evenly, from about 0.41 to 0.90. There are no outlier dots in either group. Overall, the plot shows that democracies tend to have much higher human development than non-democracies.

### Stats and description

```{r}
Democracy_HDI_summary <- FullData_2025 |>
  group_by(Democracy) |>
  summarize(avg_hdi = mean(HDI),
            sd_hdi = sd(HDI),
            min_hdi = min(HDI),
            max_hdi = max(HDI),
            mdn_hdi = median(HDI),
            iqr_hdi = IQR(HDI),
            count = n())

Democracy_HDI_summary
```

This table summarizes HDI for 73 democracies and 85 non-democracies. Democracies score higher. Their mean is about 0.845, compared with about 0.644 for non-democracies. The medians show the same gap, at about 0.878 for democracies and about 0.628 for non-democracies. That is a difference of about 0.25 in the median. In the democracy group, the mean is below the median, which points to left skew. A few lower scores pull the mean down. In the non-democracy group, the mean and median are close, so the values are more balanced. Democracies are also more consistent. Their standard deviation is about 0.104 and their IQR is about 0.154. For non-democracies, these are about 0.131 and 0.228. The ranges overlap. The lowest democracy scores about 0.550 and the highest scores about 0.972. The lowest non-democracy scores about 0.414 and the highest scores about 0.900. So the best non-democracy scores higher than the typical democracy, and the weakest democracy scores close to the typical non-democracy. Overall, democracies tend to have higher and more consistent human development. This shows a link, not a cause.The boxes barely overlap and there are no outliers, so HDI separates the groups best

## Variable 4: People in Poverty

### Graph and description

```{r}
FullData_2025 |>
  ggplot(aes(x = Poverty, y = Democracy)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::comma) +
  labs(x = "People in Poverty (log scale)",
       y = "Democracy",
       title = "Democracy vs. People in Poverty, 2025")
```

This boxplot compares the number of people in poverty for democracies and non-democracies. The x axis is on a log scale, so each step to the right is 10 times bigger. This spreads out the small values, and now we can see the democracy box, which was squeezed against zero before. The democracy box is to the left of the non-democracy box. The median is about 48,600 for democracies and about 1.2 million for non-democracies. So the typical non-democracy has about 25 times more people in poverty. The boxes overlap a little, but most democracies have far fewer people in poverty. The non-democracy box is also wider, so those countries are more spread out. The numbers are counts of people, not percents, so big countries will have bigger numbers. This is part of why the values go from as small as 23 and 119 up to about 54 million for the top democracy and about 96 million for the top non-democracy. The log scale makes the biggest values look closer to the rest than they really are, so the table shows the true size. Overall, non-democracies tend to have more people in poverty, but the groups overlap, and population size likely plays a part. The groups overlap, and the numbers depend on country size, so it is a weak predictor.

### Stats and description

```{r}
Democracy_Poverty_summary <- FullData_2025 |>
  group_by(Democracy) |>
  summarize(avg_co2 = mean(Poverty),
            sd_poverty = sd(Poverty),
            min_poverty = min(Poverty),
            max_poverty = max(Poverty),
            mdn_poverty = median(Poverty),
            iqr_poverty = IQR(Poverty),
            count = n())

Democracy_Poverty_summary

```

This table summarizes the number of people in poverty for 73 democracies and 85 non-democracies. Non-democracies have higher numbers. Their mean is about 7.9 million, compared with about 2.0 million for democracies. The medians show a much bigger gap. The median is about 1.23 million for non-democracies and only about 48,600 for democracies. So the typical non-democracy has about 25 times more people in poverty than the typical democracy. In both groups, the mean is far above the median. For non-democracies, it is about six times higher. For democracies, it is about forty times higher. A few very large countries pull the means up, so the median is a better measure of a typical country here. Non-democracies also vary more in the middle. Their IQR is about 8.0 million, compared with about 468,000 for democracies. But the standard deviation is large in both groups, about 16.4 million for non-democracies and about 7.2 million for democracies. In both cases, it is bigger than the mean, which is a sign of strong right skew. The ranges are wide. The smallest values are tiny, at 119 for non-democracies and 23 for democracies. The largest are about 95.6 million for non-democracies and about 54.2 million for democracies. Overall, non-democracies have more people in poverty, but a few huge countries drive the averages in both groups. This is a link, not a cause.

## Which variable for single variable models?

From your exploratory data analysis, which variable will you use for the single variable models? Why?

I will use HDI for the single variable models. HDI separates democracies from non-democracies better than the other variables. The median HDI is about 0.878 for democracies and about 0.628 for non-democracies, and the two boxes barely overlap. HDI has no outliers, and both groups have a similar spread. The other variables are harder to use. CO2 and Poverty are counts that depend on how big a country is, and they are very skewed with huge outliers. GDP per capita separates the groups well, but it is skewed and has high outliers. HDI already includes income, along with health and education.


## kNN classification

```{r}
#Splitting Data

#setting seed for reproducability
set.seed(2005)

#making split
FullData_2025_parts <- FullData_2025 |> 
  initial_split(prop = 0.8)

#getting training data
FullData_2025_train <- FullData_2025_parts |>
  training() 

#getting testing data
FullData_2025_test <- FullData_2025_parts |>
  testing() 

#checking sizes could do seperately and avoid list
list(FullData_2025_train, FullData_2025_test) |>
  map_int(nrow)

#Cross Validation Folds
folds <- vfold_cv(FullData_2025_train, v = 5) #this makes the folds
folds

#Setting classification metrics
classification_metrics <- metric_set(accuracy, yardstick::sensitivity,yardstick::specificity )
```

### Single variable model

Make a kNN model using your best predictor variable

```{r}
#Recipe
knn_recipe_single <- recipe(Democracy ~ HDI, data = FullData_2025_train) |>
  step_string2factor(all_nominal_predictors()) |> #From ai
  step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors())|>
  step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors())

#Specification
knn_spec_single <- nearest_neighbor(neighbors=tune(),  weight_func = "rectangular") |>
  set_engine("kknn")|>
  set_mode("classification")

#Workflow
knn_wf_single<-workflow()|>
  add_recipe(knn_recipe_single)|>
  add_model(knn_spec_single)
```

#### Model tuning to find k

```{r}
#Tuning Grid
knn_grid_single <- tibble(neighbors = seq(from=1, to=41, by=2))

knn_cv_single <- tune_grid(
  knn_wf_single,
  resamples = folds,
  grid = knn_grid_single,
  metrics = classification_metrics
)
cv_metrics_knn_single<-collect_metrics(knn_cv_single)
cv_metrics_knn_single

#Grabbing best k
best_k_single <- select_best(knn_cv_single, metric = "accuracy")
best_k_single
```

#### Model for best k

```{r}
#Specification for best k
knn_spec_single_best <- nearest_neighbor(neighbors=25, weight_func = "rectangular") |>
  set_engine("kknn")|>
  set_mode("classification")

#Workflow for best k
knn_wf_single_best<-workflow()|>
  add_recipe(knn_recipe_single)|>
  add_model(knn_spec_single_best)

#Fitting model
knn_fit_single <- 
  knn_wf_single_best |> 
  fit(data = FullData_2025_train)
knn_fit_single
```

#### Model evaluation-accuracy, cv for overfitting

```{r}
#Accuracy and overfitting assessment

#Accuracy
test_results_knn_single <- augment(knn_fit_single, new_data = FullData_2025_test)

test_knn_metrics_single<-accuracy(test_results_knn_single, truth = Democracy, estimate = .pred_class)

test_knn_metrics_single

#CV overfitting check
cv_best_k_single=cv_metrics_knn_single|>
  filter(neighbors==25)

combined_metrics_knn_single <- test_knn_metrics_single |>
  select(.metric, knn_estimate=.estimate) |>
  left_join(
    cv_best_k_single |> select(.metric, cvknn_estimate = mean),
    by = ".metric"
  ) |>
  rename(
    `Test Set` = knn_estimate,
    `CV Mean`        = cvknn_estimate
  )

combined_metrics_knn_single
```

### All variable model

Make a kNN model using all your predictor variables

```{r}
#Recipe: From lecture 14 + ai
knn_recipe_all <- recipe(Democracy ~ ., data = FullData_2025_train) |>
  update_role(geo, name, new_role = "ID") |> #From ai
  step_string2factor(all_nominal_predictors()) |> #From ai
  step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors())|>
```

#### Model tuning to find k using cv.

```{r}

cv_metrics_knn_all<-collect_metrics(knn_cv_all)
cv_metrics_knn_all

best_k_all
```

#### Model for best k

```{r}

knn_spec_all_best <- nearest_neighbor(neighbors=7,  weight_func = "rectangular") |>
  set_engine("kknn")|>
  set_mode("classification")

#Workflow for best k
knn_wf_all_best<-workflow()|>

#Fitting model
knn_fit_all <- 
  knn_wf_all_best |>
```

#### Model evaluation-accuracy, cv for overfitting

```{r}
#Accuracy and overfitting assessment

#Accuracy
test_results_knn_all <- augment(knn_fit_all, new_data = FullData_2025_test)

test_knn_metrics_all<-accuracy(test_results_knn_all, truth = Democracy, estimate = .pred_class)

test_knn_metrics_all

#CV overfitting check
cv_best_k_all=cv_metrics_knn_all|>
  filter(neighbors==7)

combined_metrics_knn_all <- test_knn_metrics_all |>
  select(.metric, knn_estimate=.estimate) |>
  left_join(
    cv_best_k_all |> select(.metric, cvknn_estimate = mean),
    by = ".metric"
  ) |>
  rename(
    `Test Set` = knn_estimate,
    `CV Mean`        = cvknn_estimate
  )

combined_metrics_knn_all
```

### Which model was best?

Of your two kNN models which performed the best? Why? If it was the multivariate model was it worth the trade off of complexity? Why?

The multivariate knn classification model performed the best because it had an accuracy of 87.5% on the test data. It was worth the trade off of complexity in this case because the single variable model only had an accuracy of 78.1% on the test data. There is a \~10% discrepancy between the multivariate test data accuracy and the cross validation estimate, but this does not indicate that the model is overfitting since the test data accuracy is higher than the cross validation estimate.


## Logistic Regression

### Single variable model

Make a logistic regression model using your best predictor variable

#### Model

```{r}
#recipe
log_rec<-
  recipe(Democracy~ HDI, data=FullData_2025_train)

#setting engine
logit_mod <-
  logistic_reg()|>
  set_engine("glm")|>
  set_mode("classification")

# workflow
glm_workflow <-
  workflow() |>
  add_recipe(log_rec)|>
  add_model(logit_mod)

# fitting model
dem_fit <-
  glm_workflow |>
  fit(data = FullData_2025_train)
```

#### Equation and Graph of model

*Equation:* $log(\frac{\hat{p}}{1-\hat{p}}=-10.09596+13.37363x_{HDI})$

```{r}
# GRAPH
FullData_bin <- FullData_2025_train |>
  mutate(bin_dem=if_else(Democracy=="Yes",1,0))

ggplot(FullData_bin, aes(x = HDI, y = bin_dem)) + 
  geom_point(
    position = position_jitter(width = 0, height = 0.05), 
    alpha = 0.5
  ) + 
  geom_smooth(
    method = "glm", method.args = list(family = "binomial"), 
    color = "dodgerblue", lty = 2, se = FALSE
  ) + 
  geom_hline(aes(yintercept = 0.5), linetype = 3) 

```

#### Model evaluation-p-values, accuracy, cv for overfitting, roc, auc

```{r}
# p-value
tidy(dem_fit) 

# Accuracy
test_results <- augment(dem_fit, new_data = FullData_2025_test) # adding original data

test_metric<-test_results|>
  accuracy(truth = Democracy, estimate = .pred_class)
test_metric

# CV for Overfitting
set.seed(2005)
folds <- vfold_cv(FullData_2025_train, v = 5) #this makes the folds
class_met=metric_set(accuracy)

glm_dem_cv <- 
  glm_workflow |> 
  fit_resamples(resamples = folds,
    metrics = class_met)

cv_metrics<-collect_metrics(glm_dem_cv)
cv_metrics

# ROC & AUC
autoplot(roc_curve(test_results, truth = Democracy, `.pred_No`)) # ROC Graph
roc_auc(test_results, truth = Democracy, `.pred_No`) # AUC 

```

**p-value:**

$p-value=1.129828e-08$

Since the p-value of the `HDI` very small (threshold: $p<=0.05$), we can say that the slope is significantly different from 0. Therefore it is *statistically significant*.

**Accuracy:** 0.8125

This tells us that our current model correctly identifies true outcomes (democracy=Yes) for approximately 81.25% of cases.

**CV for Overfitting:**

From our CV, we got 0.7781538. We can say that it is unlikely that our model overfit as 0.7781538 is reasonably close to 0.8125.

**ROC & AUC:**

$AUC=0.9365079$

We can evaluate the quality of the ROC from the area under the curve (AUC). From the graph we can see that the ROC is pretty good as it is above the 0.5 threshold which means the model performs better than a 50/50 guess and is somewhat close to the upper edge of the graph. The AUC tells us that the area under the curve is approximately 0.94 which tells us that the performance of the model is quite strong since it is close to AUC=1.0 which is a model that makes perfect predictions.

### All variable model

Make a logistic regression model using all your predictor variables

#### Model

```{r}
# Create list of only predictor variables
predictors <- colnames(FullData_2025)[4:8]

#recipe
log_rec<-
  recipe(as.formula(paste("Democracy ~", paste(predictors, collapse = " + "))),
         data=FullData_2025_train)

#setting engine
logit_mod <-
  logistic_reg()|>
  set_engine("glm")|>
  set_mode("classification")

# workflow
glm_workflow2 <-
  workflow() |>
  add_recipe(log_rec)|>
  add_model(logit_mod)

# fitting model
demMulti_fit <-
  glm_workflow2 |>
  fit(data = FullData_2025_train)

```

#### Equation of model

*Equation:* $log(\frac{\hat{p}}{1-\hat{p}}=-12.59693+17.45064x_{HDI}+0.000007621737 x_{GDP}+0.00000002082547    x_{Poverty}+0.0006021593x_{CO2}-0.04838529x_{americas}-1.787578x_{asia}-1.825651x_{europe})$

#### Model evaluation-p-values, accuracy, cv for overfitting, roc, auc

```{r}
# p-value
tidy(demMulti_fit) 

# Accuracy
test_results <- augment(demMulti_fit, new_data = FullData_2025_test) # adding original data

test_metric<-test_results|>
  accuracy(truth = Democracy, estimate = .pred_class)
test_metric

# CV for Overfitting
set.seed(2005)
folds <- vfold_cv(FullData_2025_train, v = 5) #this makes the folds
class_met=metric_set(accuracy)

glm_demMulti_cv <- 
  glm_workflow2 |> 
  fit_resamples(resamples = folds,
    metrics = class_met)

cv_metrics<-collect_metrics(glm_demMulti_cv)
cv_metrics

# ROC & AUC
autoplot(roc_curve(test_results, truth = Democracy, `.pred_No`)) # ROC Graph
roc_auc(test_results, truth = Democracy, `.pred_No`) # AUC 

```

**p-value:**

*Full Model:* $p-value=0.0003392719$

Since the p-value of the model is very small (threshold: $p<=0.05$), we can say that there is at least one predictor variable that is significantly different from 0. Therefore it is *statistically significant*.

*CO2:* $p-value=0.4498042290$

Since the p-value of the `CO2` is not considered small (threshold: $p<=0.05$), we *cannot* say that the slope is significantly different from 0. Therefore it is NOT *statistically significant*.

*GDP:* $0.7221149867$

Since the p-value of the `GDP` is not considered small (threshold: $p<=0.05$), we *cannot* say that the slope is significantly different from 0. Therefore it is NOT *statistically significant*.

*HDI:* $p-value=0.0012223916$

Since the p-value of the `HDI` very small (threshold: $p<=0.05$), we can say that the slope is significantly different from 0. Therefore it is *statistically significant*.

*Poverty:* $p-value=0.3670983647$

Since the p-value of the `Poverty` is not considered small (threshold: $p<=0.05$), we *cannot* say that the slope is significantly different from 0. Therefore it is NOT *statistically significant*.

*Regions: NOTE-* As long as one of the categorical indicators has slope significantly different from zero, then we include in the model.

*americas:* $p-value=0.9511431885$

Since the p-value of the `americas` region is not considered small (threshold: $p<=0.05$), we *cannot* say that the slope for `americas` region vs `africa` region is significantly different from zero.

*asia:* $p-value=0.0372680967$

Since the p-value of the `asia` region is very small (threshold: $p<=0.05$), we can say that the slope for `asia` region vs `africa` region is significantly different from zero.

*europe:* $p-value=0.0775613480$

Since the p-value of the `europe` region is not considered small (threshold: $p<=0.05$), we *cannot* say that the slope for `europe` region vs `africa` region is significantly different from zero.

**Accuracy:** 0.8125

This tells us that our current model correctly identifies true outcomes (democracy=Yes) for approximately 81.25% of cases.

**CV for Overfitting:**

From our CV, we got 0.7461538. We can see that there is a larger difference compared to our testing accuracy of 0.7461538. This difference may suggest some amount of overfitting; however, it is not sufficient on its own to say that the model overfit.

**ROC & AUC:**

$AUC=0.9206349$

We can evaluate the quality of the ROC from the area under the curve (AUC). From the graph we can see that the ROC is pretty good as it is above the 0.5 threshold which means the model performs better than a 50/50 guess and is somewhat close to the upper edge of the graph. The AUC tells us that the area under the curve is approximately 0.92 which tells us that the performance of the model is quite strong since it is close to AUC=1.0 which is a model that makes perfect predictions.

### Which model was best?

Of your two logistic regression models which performed the best? Why? If it was the multivariate model was it worth the trade off of complexity? Why?

The *single variable* logistic regression model performed the best overall. We can see that both models held the same testing accuracy (81.25%), but the Cross Validation accuracy for the single variable model (77.81%) is higher than that of the multivariable model (74.62%). This tells us that both models where fairly comparable in their accuracy performance; however, the single variable model performed better when it came to how well the model was able to generalize to unseen data from the CV folds.

On top of that, the AUC of the single variable model (0.94) is also higher than the AUC for the multivariable model (0.92). This is important since this metric tells us the model quality. Since the single variable model has a higher AUC, we can say that the model makes better predictions in comparison to the multivariable model.

Therefore, the single variable logistic regression model performed the best.

## Best model

Which model would you recommend the lab use? Why? Are there trade-offs between interpretability and model metrics?

We recommend using the *KNN Multivariable Classification model* for the lab. We make this recommendation based upon its performance metrics. The KNN model has a higher testing accuracy (87.50%) and cross validation accuracy (77.08%) than the logistic regression model, which achieved a testing accuracy of 81.25% and cross validation accuracy of 74.62%.

We should note, however, that while the KNN model has a better overall performance, the testing accuracy and the CV accuracy show a larger difference in percentage (approx. 10%) in comparison to the logistic regression model which only has as differnece of approximately 6.5%. This should caution us that some overfitting may be a potential issue with the KNN model, although no strong claims can be made at this time. Another trade-off with the KNN model comes from its complexity and interpretability. Since the KNN model uses all the predictor variables, it becomes more challenging to isolate, understand, and explain how the model makes individual  predictions. In contrast, the single logistic regression model is much simpler to follow since it only follows the relationship between HDI (predictor variable) and the probability of Democracy (response variable). 

Overall, even with some of the trade-offs with the multivariable KNN classification model, we still recommend this model to be used in the lab. Its metrics are the best overall, and demonstrate that it is an effective model for the purposes of predicting the response variable (Democracy).
